The question of whether a meteor impact caused the Younger Dryas period is actively debated among scientists, with no consensus. Some researchers argue strongly for an extraterrestrial impact: a Dartmouth-led study reported "conclusive evidence" linking a comet or meteor impact with the Younger Dryas environmental transformation, based on spherules recovered from boundary layers in Pennsylvania and New Jersey [d7], and one source goes so far as to say the Younger Dryas impact "should no longer be viewed as a hypothesis but instead as an observation" [d1]. However, multiple high-credibility studies directly contradict this view: a study published in Geophysical Research Letters (American Geophysical Union) concluded that the supposed impact evidence—carbonaceous spherules and nanodiamonds—are "nothing more than fossilized balls of fungus, charcoal, and fecal pellets," and that these materials date from thousands of years both before and after the Younger Dryas onset [d2][d4]. Isotopic analysis of sediments from Hall's Cave in Texas found that key elements (iridium, ruthenium, platinum, palladium, rhenium) were not in the correct proportions for a meteor impact, instead matching volcanic gases, leading researchers to conclude the cooling was caused by "numerous coincident Earth-based processes, not an extraterrestrial impact" [d5][d8]. Additionally, the Hiawatha crater in Greenland, once considered a candidate, has been dated to approximately 58 million years ago, ruling it out as a Younger Dryas cause [d6], while other researchers have proposed that freshwater influx into the North Atlantic, changes in ocean circulation, or volcanic eruptions were responsible [d3][d4][d5].
